newsitem.title: UK: UK Q2 GDP said to push further above trend rate.
newsitem.headline: UK Q2 GDP said to push further above trend rate.

text.p: British economic growth is expected to have pushed further above the trend rate in the second quarter, driven in large part by the consumer, economists said on Thursday.

Preliminary GDP figures for the period are due at 0830 GMT on Friday and will be keenly watched as the last set of significant data before the Bank of England's monetary policy committee meets again on August 6 and 7 to discuss the level of interest rates.

The Reuter consensus forecast suggests GDP grew 0.9 percent quarter-on-quarter, the same as in the first quarter, pushing year-on-year growth to 3.4 percent from 3.1 percent in the first. The trend rate of growth is estimated to be around 2.5 percent.

"The numbers are likely to be watched quite closely to determine whether the increasing strength in consumer activity has been matched by the overall economy," said Dharshini David, UK economist at HSBC Markets.
"A strong figure might well add to the case for a further increase in base rates."
Figures out on Wednesday showed retail sales grew by 1.8 percent in the quarter, signalling increasingly strong activity in the consumer sector, possibly boosted by windfall payments.
"If that is copied across to consumer spending as a whole, we will be looking at second-quarter growth well in excess of one percent," said Andrew Snowball, UK economist at the Co-operative Bank.
With consumer spending accelerating, output should have expanded sharply, too. But economists said only service sector output was likely to have kept pace.

"Weakness in construction orders and private housing starts suggests that construction output is unlikely to have risen as strongly as it did in the first quarter," said Michael Saunders, UK economist at Salomon Brothers.
He forecast quarterly growth of 0.8 as a result.
Latest industrial production figures show that sector, too, will act as a drag on the output total.
In May, manufacturing output fell by 1.1 percent and, even allowing for a partial rebound in June, output from the sector would be about flat in the quarter, David said.

"And even with a large rebound in energy, industrial production appears unlikely to grow by more than a quarter percent in the quarter, an extremely modest expansion compared to the one we expect to see in service sector output," she added.
But Snowball said that barring a huge jump in growth, the central bank would hold off and not raise rates in August.

"We have had four rate rises in nine months. The Bank is well aware that some of the spending effects are temporary and that the pound has gone from strength to strength in that time. It has even put on 2.5 percent since the last meeting," he said.
